newsitem.title: UK: Siebe says APV to enhance earnings.
newsitem.headline: Siebe says APV to enhance earnings.

text.p: British controls systems group Siebe Plc on Friday made a 327.4 million pound ($531.7 million) offer for process engineering group APV which it said would be immediately earnings enhancing.

"It is earnings enhancing right out of the blocks," Siebe's chief executive Allen Yurko told Reuters. He said the offer represented a 59 percent premium for APV shareholders and had the blessing of both boards.

The offer of 0.10955 new Siebe shares for each APV share values APV shares at approximately 105 pence each but there is a full cash alternative of 97.5 pence per APV share. Yurko said this would be 50 percent underwritten by Siebe itself.
"There is an unassailable strategic and industrial logic for Siebe," Yurko said. "We see this as more of a growth acquisition than a pure turn-around play."
Analysts said the acquisition looked a good fit with Siebe's existing businesses but the price it was paying could be hard to justify.

"The industrial logic is fairly sound," said Chris Hemingway, analyst at Lehman Brothers, "the way Siebe has been developing meant the food industry has become a big new potential market and APV was already a competitor."
Hemingway said the price was 20 times APV's historic earnings and some 2.75 times the book value of its assets.
Yurko denied the deal was overpriced. "Its a good price for the their shares. It is not overpriced."
By taking over APV, Siebe will add more than 1000 people in sales and engineering, giving it a significant presence in providing control systems to food, beverage, dairy and pharmaceuticals plants.

"This is a direct bold stroke at the food, beverage and pharmaceutical industry," Yurko said, adding that the integration of APV into Siebe Control Systems would be completed within six months if the deal goes ahead.
Siebe and APV said significant cost benefits were expected by combining their global networks of local engineering, contracting and customer service organisations.
But Yurko declined to say how many staff might lose their jobs. He said the deal "could mean some additional reductions in staff". APV has already shaved its workforce from around 13,000 to 7,000.
And APV's management would be given due consideration in Siebe's plans for the business, he added.

In a joint statement the two firms said the deal would unlock significant growth potential for APV by introducing Siebe's Foxboro Intelligent Automation System into APV's product range as well as adding sales and engineering staff to sell and install Siebe's new Intelligent Automation Windows NT system.
The deal would also widen Siebe Control Systems' core products to include APV valves, pumps and heat exchangers, the firms said.

APV's chairman Mike Smith said that following several years of restructuring "designed to concentrate APV's business and improve operational efficiency", APV was better positioned for 1997 and beyond.
Smith said APV's businesses and employees would have the opportunity to benefit from being part of the larger Siebe group and customers would benefit from the enlarged product range.

APV said it had received an indication of interest that might result in an offer for the company on April 29. Siebe already owns 8.9 APV shares, almost three percent of the company and has undertakings from APV directors for another 0.1 percent.
Yurko said Siebe would be looking at other acquisitions, but stressed that the APV offer represented "a good clip on" at around only seven percent of Siebe's 4.5 billion pound market capitalisation.
"We are always looking at a variety of small and medium opportunities," he said, adding that there was nothing in immediate prospect.
Siebe's shares were down 21 pence at 937.5 pence at 0856 GMT, while APV's shares were up 14.5 pence at 104 pence. ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
